1.pericope_label: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord... But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports Luther's judgment that this is among the Pauline psalms and places it sixth of the seven penitential; Ellicott alone works the philology of the third verse, showing that the word rendered mark is the one rendered watch two verses later, corrects the conjunction of the fourth verse from but to for, and raises the possibility that the fear intended is struck in the heathen rather than in the forgiven.

Gill refuses the literal reading of the depths and settles on a deep sense of sin, and runs through what it would mean for God to mark iniquities; Calvin allows either the psalmist or the whole Church, and turns aside to attack the recitation of the psalm for the dead.

Clarke dates the psalm to the captivity on the ground that it has no title in any version, and answers the third verse with the warning that but for the fourth none could be saved; Wesley specifies a childlike rather than a slavish fear and calls this mercy the foundation of all religion.

Henry hears in the doubled naming of God a dread of his wrath and draws three lessons from it, and insists that the forgiveness is given not to be presumed upon but that God may be worshipped; Spurgeon makes the location of the prayer the point, since deep places beget deep devotion.
Augustine takes Jonah as the pattern and then turns the deep inward, holding that this mortal life is the deep and that those are furthest down in it who do not cry from it at all.

positions.view: This mortal life itself; the deepest are those who do not cry out of it.
A deep sense of sin, under which a man sees himself unworthy.
The captivity, the exiles being as men in a pit.
Extreme danger of body or mind, whether the psalmist's own or the Church's.
A recurrent image for overwhelming distress, used literally of the sea.

debates.question: Why is there forgiveness, that God may be feared?

positions.view: So that God may be worshipped, since sinners could have no dealings with a master who passed by nothing.
A childlike and not a slavish fear; this mercy is the foundation of all religion.
Either that the forgiven become more profoundly religious, or that the heathen are struck with fear at the mercy shown to Israel.

outliers.note: Interrupts the exposition to attack the Roman recitation of this psalm for the dead, arguing that once the deep was taken for purgatory the psalm was believed to be of no use to the living.
Observes that the word for marking iniquities is the same as the word for watching for the dawn, so that God watching for men's lapses would be the mirror image of the psalmist watching for him.

themes: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord.
Lord, hear my voice: let thine ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications.
If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?
But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared.

5.pericope_label: I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope... And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities

schools.summary: Ellicott catches the tense of the waiting, that the psalmist has been waiting and waits still, offers the Levite sentinel who signalled the dawn for the temple rites, presses the emphatic pronoun of the last verse, and argues from a parallel psalm that this one deliberately asks deliverance from sin and not only from its consequences.
Gill lists what is waited for and suggests David may have waited for the coming of Christ, and extends the iniquities of the last verse to the original and the actual, the secret and the open.

Clarke derives the verb for waiting from the stretching of a cord between two points, suspects the text of the sixth verse and canvasses three renderings of it, fastens on the emphatic Hebrew article in mercy and redemption, and refuses to restrict the closing promise to Israel in Babylon; Wesley allows the watchers to be either soldiers or temple priests.

Henry hears the repetition as a climax proper to a song of ascents, grounds the hope strictly on what God has promised, works the comparison with the watchers in two directions, and divides the redemption into its nature, its riches and its persons.

debates.question: Who are they that watch for the morning?

positions.view: Sentinels on the walls, watchers with the sick, and travellers abroad at night.
Either soldiers keeping the night watches or the priests who did so in the temple.
Perhaps the Levite sentinel who signalled the first ray of dawn, though the figure is striking taken generally.
The text itself is doubtful; it may mean those observing the watches in order to offer the oblation, or from morning watch to morning watch, that is, day and night.

debates.question: How far does the closing promise of redemption reach?

positions.view: To the whole elect, from iniquities original and actual, secret and open.
Not to Israel in Babylon only; every believer may take it to himself.
To deliverance from sin itself and not merely from its consequences, which is what marks the psalm as penitential.
To Israel according to the spirit, and from the commanding as well as the condemning power of sin.

outliers.note: Derives the verb for waiting from the extension of a cord from one point to another, making God one point and the human heart the other with believing desire stretched between them.
Records a quite different rendering of the sixth verse under which the soul hastens to the Lord from the morning guards, meaning daily prayer at the hour of the morning sacrifice.

themes: I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope.
My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
Let Israel hope in the Lord: for with the Lord there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption.
And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
